::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
### Quick start

If someone has already set up MicroCPipe on your cluster and you just want a
run, these are the steps. Each one is explained in the sections below.

1. Clone the repository and `cd` into it ([Setup](#one-time-setup)).
2. Describe your FASTQ files in `MicroCSamplesheet.txt`
   ([Samplesheet](#describe-your-sequencing-runs)).
3. Point `config/MicroCConfig.yaml` at your reference
   ([Config](#point-the-config-at-your-reference)).
4. Set `MICROC_PROFILE` and `MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT` in `~/.bashrc`
   ([Compute site](#tell-microcpipe-which-cluster-you-are-on)).
5. Dry run: `bash MicroCPipe.sh -n` ([Dry run](#dry-run)).
6. Run: `sbatch MicroCPipe.sh`, then open `output/qc/MicroC_qc_report.html`
   ([Run](#run-it), [QC](#read-the-qc-dashboard)).
7. Load the maps from `output/<group>/` ([Inspecting](#inspecting-the-outputs)).
:::

This page is a single walkthrough. The other chapters are reference pages;
this one takes you from an empty directory to a finished run and a look at
the maps, in the order you would do things. **Every code block here is
illustrative and is not executed when the book is built: no output shown on
this page comes from a real run, and the paths and names are placeholders.**

## The example

You have one Micro-C library from a human cell line (here called `GM12878`),
sequenced once, with the FASTQ files `MicroC_2M_R1.fastq.gz` and
`MicroC_2M_R2.fastq.gz` in a folder on your cluster. You want the contact
maps in cooler and Juicebox formats and a check that the library is good.

## One-time setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jpflores-13/MicroCPipe.git
cd MicroCPipe
```

You need `python3` >= 3.11 and `conda` >= 24.7.1 on the cluster, a BWA-indexed
FASTA of the reference and a chromosome sizes file ([Setup](setup.qmd)).

## Describe your sequencing runs

`MicroCSamplesheet.txt` is tab-separated, with one row per sequencing run:

```
Name                Project  Cell_Type  Condition  Bio_Rep  Tech_Rep  Seq_Rep  Read1                  Read2                  Sequencing_Directory
GM12878_ctrl_1_1_1  Example  GM12878    Ctrl       1        1         1        MicroC_2M_R1.fastq.gz  MicroC_2M_R2.fastq.gz  /path/to/raw/
```

With the default `mergeBy` (`Project`, `Cell_Type`, `Bio_Rep`, `Tech_Rep`),
the group for this row is `Example_GM12878_1_1`, and all outputs will be in
`output/Example_GM12878_1_1/`. If you sequenced the same library a second
time, add a second row with `Seq_Rep` 2: both rows share the group, are
aligned separately, then merged and deduplicated together.

## Point the config at your reference

In `config/MicroCConfig.yaml`:

```yaml
genome: 'hg38'
fasta: '/path/to/hg38/BWAIndex/genome.fa'
chromSizes: '/path/to/hg38.chrom.sizes'
outputs: ['cool', 'mcool', 'hic']
```

`chromSizes` should list only the chromosomes you want in the maps, with
the same names as the FASTA. Leave the rest at their defaults for a first run.

## Tell MicroCPipe which cluster you are on

Once per cluster, in `~/.bashrc`:

```bash
export MICROC_PROFILE=profiles/biowulf          # or longleaf, pioneer, local, your own
export MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT=/data/$USER/MicroCPipe  # big files go here
```

Then `source ~/.bashrc`, and open `profiles/<site>/config.yaml` to check the
account and partition are yours ([Cluster Reference](cluster.qmd)).

## Dry run

Before submitting anything, list what would run:

```bash
bash MicroCPipe.sh -n
```

This reads the samplesheet and config, checks that the FASTQ files exist, and
prints each job. For this example, the workflow graph implies one job per
rule, twelve in all (including the final `all`):

| Rule | Jobs |
|------|------|
| `align`, `dedup`, `split`, `sort_bam` | 1 each |
| `qc_summary`, `library_complexity` | 1 each |
| `cool`, `mcool`, `hic` | 1 each |
| `benchmark_summary`, `qc_report`, `all` | 1 each |

(A second sequencing row would make it two `align` jobs and still one of
everything else.) If the dry run stops with a missing-column error, a
`MissingInputException` or a resolution error, fix it now: see the
troubleshooting tables in [Setup](setup.qmd).

The first run builds four conda environments. If you want to do that on a
compute node rather than inside the launcher job:

```bash
srun -N 1 -n 1 -c 4 --mem=16g -t 3:00:00 --pty /bin/bash
bash MicroCPipe.sh --conda-create-envs-only
exit
```

## Run it

```bash
sbatch MicroCPipe.sh
```

Each rule is submitted as its own SLURM job. Watch them with
`squeue -u $USER`; the launcher's own log is `MicroCPipe-<jobid>.out` and
each job's log is in `$MICROC_OUTPUT_ROOT/output/<group>/logs/`. If you set
`MICROC_EMAIL` you also get mail when it starts, finishes or fails
([Running](running.qmd#email-notifications)).

If something fails, read that job's log, fix the cause (often memory or
time in the profile), then:

```bash
bash unlock.sh
sbatch MicroCPipe.sh
```

Finished jobs are kept ([Running](running.qmd#resuming-and-re-running)).

## Read the QC dashboard

Copy `output/qc/MicroC_qc_report.html` to your computer (or open it where you
are) and look at, in this order:

1. The **Summary** table: any red or amber cells?
2. **Library composition**: how is the library split into unique, unmapped
   and duplicate pairs, cis and trans, short and long cis?
3. **P(s)** and **strand orientation**: smooth long-range decay, and
   orientations that settle toward balanced with distance.
4. **Library complexity**: is more depth worth it?

[Reading the QC dashboard](qc.qmd) explains each panel and what failure looks
like. Decide here whether the library is worth analysing before you spend
time on the maps.

## Inspecting the outputs

```
output/Example_GM12878_1_1/
├── Example_GM12878_1_1.pairs.gz
├── Example_GM12878_1_1.cool
├── Example_GM12878_1_1.mcool
├── Example_GM12878_1_1.hic
├── Example_GM12878_1_1_dedup_stats.txt
├── Example_GM12878_1_1_mapped.PT.bam(.bai)
├── Example_GM12878_1_1_qc_summary.txt
└── Example_GM12878_1_1_libraryComplexity.txt
```

### With the cooler command line

```bash
M=output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.mcool
cooler ls $M                                   # lists the resolutions
cooler info $M::resolutions/10000               # bins, pixels, chromosome sizes
cooler dump --join -r chr1:1,000,000-3,000,000 $M::resolutions/10000 | head
```

### In Python

```python
import cooler, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

clr = cooler.Cooler("output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.mcool::resolutions/10000")
region = "chr1:1,000,000-3,000,000"
mat = clr.matrix(balance=True).fetch(region)     # needs an .mcool level (the base .cool has no weights); balance=False for raw counts
plt.imshow(mat, cmap="YlOrRd", norm=LogNorm())
plt.colorbar(label="balanced contact frequency")
plt.show()
```

Expected contact frequency (the P(s) curve) from the same file, using
cooltools:

```python
import cooltools
exp = cooltools.expected_cis(clr, nproc=4)       # one row per distance bin and chromosome arm
```

The unique, deduplicated read pairs (pair types UU, UR, RU) are a plain table if you want something else:

```python
import pandas as pd
cols = ["readID", "chrom1", "pos1", "chrom2", "pos2", "strand1", "strand2", "pair_type"]
pairs = pd.read_csv("output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.pairs.gz",
                    sep="\t", comment="#", header=None, usecols=range(8), names=cols)
```

### In R

With Bioconductor's HiCExperiment package (`.cool` / `.mcool`):

```r
library(HiCExperiment)
cf  <- CoolFile("output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.mcool", resolution = 10000)
hic <- import(cf, focus = "chr1:1000000-3000000")
plotMatrix(hic, use.scores = "balanced")
```

Or read the `.hic` with strawr:

```r
library(strawr)
x <- straw("KR", "output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.hic",
           "chr1", "chr1", "BP", 10000)
head(x)   # columns x, y, counts
```

(`straw` needs a normalisation name the file contains; `"NONE"` always
works.)

### In Juicebox

Open Juicebox, choose **File > Open > Local** and select
`Example_GM12878_1_1.hic`. Pick a normalisation and resolution from the menus.

## Combining libraries

Suppose you made a second technical replicate (`Tech_Rep` 2) and ran it
through the Core workflow too. To merge the two into one deeper map, list
their pairs in `MicroCMergeSamplesheet.txt`:

```
Name              Project  Cell_Type  Condition  Bio_Rep  Tech_Rep  pairs
GM12878_ctrl_1_1  Example  GM12878    Ctrl       1        1         output/Example_GM12878_1_1/Example_GM12878_1_1.pairs.gz
GM12878_ctrl_1_2  Example  GM12878    Ctrl       1        2         output/Example_GM12878_1_2/Example_GM12878_1_2.pairs.gz
```

With the default `merge: mergeBy` (no `Tech_Rep`), both rows form one group,
`merged_Example_GM12878_1` (the Merge workflow prefixes its groups with
`merged_` so they never collide with Core outputs):

```bash
bash MicroCMerge.sh -n
sbatch MicroCMerge.sh
```

The merged maps are written to `output/merged_Example_GM12878_1/` as
`merged_Example_GM12878_1.cool`, `.mcool` and `.hic`, built from
`merged_Example_GM12878_1_merged.pairs.gz`. Check the individual libraries in the
dashboard first: merging a failed library into a good one makes the deeper map
worse, not better.
